```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(sf)
  library(fixest)
  library(tmap)
  library(VancouvR)
})
tmap_mode("plot")
```

```{r}
#| label: events
#| include: false
# Event dates, as decimal years for the charts. Construction began in late
# 2005, the line opened on August 17, 2009, and Council approved phase 3 of
# the Cambie Corridor Plan on May 1, 2018.
construction_start <- decimal_date(ymd("2005-11-01"))
line_opens <- decimal_date(ymd("2009-08-17"))
rezoning <- decimal_date(ymd("2018-05-01"))
```

```{r}
#| label: data
#| include: false
# The four Canada Line stations (opened August 2009) on residential streets;
# the downtown stations replaced existing transit, so they are left out
new_stations <- c("King Edward", "Oakridge - 41st Avenue",
                  "Langara - 49th Avenue", "Marine Drive")
stations <- get_cov_data("rapid-transit-stations") |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  filter(station %in% new_stations) |>
  st_transform(26910)
stopifnot(nrow(stations) == 4)

# Single-family sales in the City of Vancouver. Prices of $100,000 or less are
# not market sales. 2026 is a partial year.
sales_sf <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds") |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", act_use_cat == "S/F Res",
         !is.na(lon), price > 100000, year(sale_date) <= 2025) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(26910)

nearest <- stations[st_nearest_feature(sales_sf, stations), ]
sales <- sales_sf |>
  mutate(dist = as.numeric(st_distance(sales_sf, nearest, by_element = TRUE))) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(dist < 2000) |>
  mutate(year = year(sale_date), age = year - year_built, near = dist < 800)
```

```{r}
#| label: models
#| include: false
# Event study: the near-station gap in each year relative to 2004, the last
# year before construction. Every 2021 sale lacks lot size and floor area, so
# the size controls drop 2021.
event_study <- function(data) {
  m <- feols(log(price) ~ i(year, near, ref = 2004) + log(lotsize) +
               log(floorarea) + age | year + neigh_label,
             data = data, cluster = ~neigh_label)
  broom::tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(str_starts(term, "year::")) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(term, "\\d{4}"))) |>
    select(year, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) |>
    bind_rows(tibble(year = 2004L, estimate = 0, conf.low = 0, conf.high = 0))
}
es_base <- event_study(sales)
es_no_luxury <- event_study(
  filter(sales, !neigh_label %in% c("Shaughnessy", "South Granville"))
)
es_500 <- event_study(
  filter(sales, dist < 1600) |> mutate(near = dist < 500)
)

avg_gap <- function(es, years) mean(es$estimate[es$year %in% years])
pct <- function(x) round(100 * (exp(x) - 1))
# Signed percentage with a typographic minus, for slide text
signed <- function(x) {
  v <- pct(x)
  if (v == 0) return("about 0%")
  paste0(if (v < 0) "\u2212" else "+", abs(v), "%")
}
open_gap <- avg_gap(es_base, 2010:2014)
rezone_gap <- avg_gap(es_base, 2016:2019)
```

## Thesis

```{r code-thesis, ref.label=c("setup", "data", "models"), eval=FALSE}
```

::: {.key-point}
The Canada Line did not raise nearby house prices when it opened in 2009. A premium of about `r pct(rezone_gap)`% appeared only in 2016–2019, as the City moved to rezone single-family lots near the stations.
:::

- **Evidence:** `r scales::comma(nrow(sales))` single-family sales near four Cambie Street stations, 2000–2025.
- **Comparison:** homes within 800 m of a station against homes 800 m to 2 km away.

::: {.notes}
Speaker 1 presents slides 2–5; Speaker 2 presents slides 6–10. About 30 seconds. Say the thesis in your own words, then tell the audience what they will see: where the stations are, why a simple comparison misleads, and when the premium appeared.
:::

## Four new stations on a residential street

```{r code-four-new-stations-on-a-residen, ref.label=c("setup", "data", "map"), eval=FALSE}
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: map
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
areas <- get_cov_data("local-area-boundary") |> st_as_sf() |> st_transform(26910)
zone_near <- st_union(st_buffer(stations, 800))
zone_far <- st_union(st_buffer(stations, 2000))
stations$label <- c("King Edward" = "King Edward",
                    "Oakridge - 41st Avenue" = "Oakridge–41st",
                    "Langara - 49th Avenue" = "Langara–49th",
                    "Marine Drive" = "Marine Drive")[stations$station]

# Labels sit 900 m east of each station, just outside its 800 m circle
labels <- stations |> mutate(geometry = st_geometry(stations) + c(900, 0)) |>
  st_set_crs(26910)

map_box <- st_bbox(zone_far)
map_box["xmax"] <- map_box["xmax"] + 1500  # room for the labels

tm_shape(areas, bbox = map_box) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey96", col = "grey75") +
  tm_shape(zone_far) + tm_borders(col = "grey35", lty = "dashed") +
  tm_shape(zone_near) + tm_polygons(fill = "#2a78d6", fill_alpha = 0.3, col = "#2a78d6") +
  tm_shape(stations) + tm_dots(fill = "black", size = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(labels) +
  tm_text("label", size = 0.9, fontface = "bold", options = opt_tm_text(just = "left")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
- **Near (blue):** within 800 m of a station, a 10-minute walk.
- **Comparison (dashed):** 800 m to 2 km away.
- Earlier studies find that rail stations raise nearby home values, often before they open.
- **New here:** the Canada Line, and separating the train from the rezoning that followed.
:::
::::

City of Vancouver Open Data: rapid transit stations, local areas
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. The previous slide made the claim; this slide shows the setting. Point to the stations. Mention the two studies on the Sources slide only briefly.
:::

## Homes near the stations always cost more

```{r code-homes-near-the-stations-always, ref.label=c("setup", "events", "data", "levels"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: levels
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
sales |>
  summarise(median = median(price), .by = c(year, near)) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(near, "Within 800 m", "800 m to 2 km")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, median / 1e6, colour = group)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = construction_start, xmax = line_opens, ymin = 0,
           ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90") +  # ymin = 0, not -Inf, on a log scale
  annotate("text", x = (construction_start + line_opens) / 2, y = 4,
           label = "Construction", size = 5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(suffix = "M", accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Within 800 m" = "#2a78d6", "800 m to 2 km" = "grey45")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Median sale price (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Near-station homes sold for more even in 2000, before the line existed. Comparing levels would credit the train for a gap that was already there.

::: footer
BC Assessment single-family sales, City of Vancouver
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. The two lines move together until about 2015. That is why the analysis compares changes, not levels: a difference in differences.
:::

## Comparing changes: no premium after opening

```{r code-comparing-changes-no-premium-a, ref.label=c("setup", "data", "did-table"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: did-table
#| echo: false
did <- sales |>
  mutate(period = case_when(year <= 2004 ~ "before",
                            between(year, 2010, 2014) ~ "after")) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  summarise(mean_log = mean(log(price)), .by = c(near, period)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = mean_log) |>
  mutate(change = after - before)
did_estimate <- did$change[did$near] - did$change[!did$near]

did |>
  arrange(desc(near)) |>
  transmute(Homes = if_else(near, "Within 800 m", "800 m to 2 km"),
            `2000–2004` = scales::dollar(exp(before), accuracy = 1000),
            `2010–2014` = scales::dollar(exp(after), accuracy = 1000),
            Change = scales::percent(exp(change) - 1, accuracy = 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

- Typical prices rose `r scales::percent(exp(did$change[did$near]) - 1)` near the stations and `r scales::percent(exp(did$change[!did$near]) - 1)` farther away.
- Difference in differences: `r signed(did_estimate)`.

::: footer
Typical price: geometric mean of single-family sale prices. Change compares 2010–2014 with 2000–2004.
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1.5 minutes. This is the difference in differences in its simplest form: the change near the stations minus the change farther away. The two changes are almost identical, so the opening added nothing. The next slide repeats this comparison year by year.
:::

## No premium at opening; a premium with rezoning

```{r code-no-premium-at-opening-a-premiu, ref.label=c("setup", "events", "data", "models", "event-study"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: event-study
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
ggplot(es_base, aes(year, estimate)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = construction_start, xmax = line_opens,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = line_opens, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rezoning, colour = "#c0392b", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = line_opens + 0.2, y = 0.33, label = "Line opens",
           hjust = 0, colour = "#2a78d6", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = rezoning + 0.2, y = 0.33, label = "Rezoning approved",
           hjust = 0, colour = "#c0392b", size = 5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Near-station price gap vs 2004") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

- 2010–2014: about `r signed(open_gap)`. 2016–2019: about `r signed(rezone_gap)`.

::: footer
Log price on year × near, with lot size, floor area, age, year and neighbourhood fixed effects. 95% intervals; 2021 lacks size data.
:::

::: {.notes}
Speaker 2 takes over here. About 1.5 minutes. This is the key slide. Before 2005 the gap is flat: the two areas moved together. During construction (shaded), near-station homes lost a few percent. After the line opened, nothing. The premium appears in 2016 and peaks in `r es_base$year[which.max(es_base$estimate)]`; Council approved the Cambie Corridor Plan's third phase, which allowed about 1,700 single-family lots to become townhouses and apartments, in May 2018. It fades later, possibly because land assemblies near the stations had already sold.
:::

## Alternative: a slump in the comparison area?

```{r code-alternative-a-slump-in-the-com, ref.label=c("setup", "data", "models"), eval=FALSE}
```

1. **The alternative:** after the 2016 foreign buyer tax, luxury homes in Shaughnessy and South Granville slumped. A weak comparison area could create a false premium.
2. **If it were true:** dropping those two areas would shrink the 2016–2019 premium.
3. **What we see:** the premium is about `r signed(avg_gap(es_no_luxury, 2016:2019))` without them, against `r signed(rezone_gap)` with them.

::: {.key-point}
The premium is not an artifact of the comparison area.
:::

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. This is the alternative a sceptical listener would raise first, because the comparison area includes some of the most expensive streets in the city.
:::

## Homes closest to the stations gained the most

```{r code-homes-closest-to-the-stations, ref.label=c("setup", "events", "data", "models", "robust-500"), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r}
#| label: robust-500
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
bind_rows(`800 m vs 800 m–2 km` = es_base, `500 m vs 500 m–1.6 km` = es_500,
          .id = "zone") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, estimate, colour = zone)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rezoning, colour = "#c0392b", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`800 m vs 800 m–2 km` = "#2a78d6",
                                 `500 m vs 500 m–1.6 km` = "#eb6834")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Near-station price gap vs 2004", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Closer homes show a larger premium at the rezoning peak, consistent with rezoning near the stations.

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. A robustness check: a narrower 500 m zone gives the same timing, with a larger peak. If the premium came from rezoning near the stations, the lots closest to them should gain most, and they do.
:::

## What this analysis cannot tell us

- **Timing, not proof.** The premium coincides with rezoning, but other changes near the stations in 2016–2018 cannot be ruled out.
- **Single-family homes only.** Condo prices near the stations may have responded differently.
- **Who buys after rezoning.** Near-station buyers after 2016 may be developers assembling land, so prices reflect redevelopment value.
- **Wide intervals.** Standard errors are clustered by only `r n_distinct(sales$neigh_label)` neighbourhoods.

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. Naming the limits yourself is more convincing than waiting for the audience to raise them.
:::

## Takeaways

- Opening the Canada Line did not lift nearby single-family prices.
- The premium came with rezoning: land near stations became worth more when the City allowed more homes on it.
- Transit's value to landowners depends on zoning. Policies that capture land value near stations should be tied to rezoning, not just to the train.

::: {.notes}
About 30 seconds. End on the policy point, then stop and take questions.
:::

## Backup: Sources {.smaller}

- Gibbons, S., and S. Machin (2005). "Valuing rail access using transport innovations." *Journal of Urban Economics* 57(1): 148–169.
- McMillen, D. P., and J. McDonald (2004). "Reaction of house prices to a new rapid transit line: Chicago's Midway Line, 1983–1999." *Real Estate Economics* 32(3): 463–486.
- City of Vancouver (2018). *Cambie Corridor Plan*, approved by Council on 1 May 2018.
- Data: BC Assessment sales (course file `bca262.rds`); City of Vancouver Open Data.

## Backup: Decision log

1. **Four stations only.** The downtown stations replaced existing transit, so they cannot show a new-station effect.
2. **800 m for "near".** A 10-minute walk. A 500 m zone gives the same pattern.
3. **2004 as the reference year.** Construction began in late 2005; earlier years test whether the two areas moved together.
4. **Found: 2021 has no lot size or floor area.** The regression silently dropped every 2021 sale. Without size controls the pattern is the same.
5. **Canada Line, not Millennium Line.** The Millennium Line opened in 2002, leaving less than three years of sales before opening.
